analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules to privately traded energy deals like oil, gas, and electricity contracts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 35 House sponsors after the 2005–2006 run-up in gasoline and natural gas prices, the bill was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2006, with gasoline and natural gas prices high, this bill would have closed a gap in federal law: contracts in oil, gasoline, coal, natural gas, and electricity traded privately between big financial players — not on public exchanges — were largely beyond the reach of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The bill would have brought those private energy deals under federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules, required large traders to report big positions and keep records regulators could inspect, required trading platforms to publish volumes and prices, and raised penalties for manipulation to as much as $1 million or triple the violator's gain, with prison terms doubled to ten years. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Agriculture Committee and one of its subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households and businesses that pay gasoline, heating fuel, natural gas, and electricity prices set in these markets. The bill aimed at traders who take large private positions that move those prices; if manipulation or hidden cornering of a market was inflating costs at the pump or the utility bill, giving the Commodity Futures Trading Commission the power to see the trades, demand records, and impose penalties would work in consumers' favor. Honest energy companies hedging real risks would also benefit from cleaner, more transparent price discovery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households paying gasoline and heating bills

how_it_helps.text: It would have given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over energy trades done privately between big players off the public exchanges, rather than only exchange-traded contracts.

It required large traders in energy deals that set market prices to report big positions to the Commission and keep five years of records open to inspection by the Commission and the Attorney General.

It extended fraud prohibitions to practices like filling a customer's order by matching it against another of the trader's own orders without consent, and it raised civil penalties for manipulation to up to $1 million or triple the violator's gain, whichever is larger, while doubling the prison term for violations from five to ten years.
It required electronic energy trading platforms to make trading volumes, settlement prices, and daily price ranges public, so traders and consumers could see what the market was actually doing.

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, hedge funds, swap dealers, and electronic trading platforms that profit from unregulated over-the-counter energy trading. They would bear new reporting and recordkeeping obligations, public disclosure of volumes and prices, and exposure to civil penalties up to the greater of $1 million or triple their gain from manipulation, plus criminal penalties with prison terms of up to ten years. Some costs of compliance could ultimately be passed into trading costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy derivatives traders and trading platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed new reporting, recordkeeping, and public-disclosure requirements on energy firms and electronic trading platforms, adding compliance costs and, under the bill's own terms, allowing the Commission discretion over which trades count as price-setting and must be reported.

Opponents of extending Commodity Exchange Act rules to over-the-counter energy trades generally argue that large commercial users need flexible private contracts to hedge real business risks, and that heavier oversight could push that trading offshore or raise hedging costs for energy producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — regulators able to see and punish manipulation in the markets that set gasoline, natural gas, and electricity prices — is real and would fall on the traders and firms that profit from opacity, not on ordinary households. The honest costs: some compliance burden on energy firms and trading platforms, and a risk that tighter reporting could nudge some derivatives trading overseas or reduce market liquidity, which could affect hedging costs that energy producers pass through. On balance, the costs are modest compared with the public cost of undetected energy price manipulation, but the bill was never debated, so its design was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on April 27, 2006, joined by 20 original cosponsors including Rep. John Dingell, after two years of rising gasoline and natural gas prices.
It gathered 34 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture on the day it was introduced, and to that committee's Farm Commodities and Risk Management Subcommittee on May 9, 2006.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy traders and dealers who traded energy contracts privately, off regulated exchanges, kept operating without federal reporting requirements or manipulation penalties, because no competing bill closed that gap in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy traders who kept the loophole

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor twice in May 2006.

for.name: Rep. John Dingell
for.role: Ranking member (later Chairman) of the Energy and Commerce Committee; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Republican-led, chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after receiving the referral; it was passed down to a subcommittee on May 9, 2006, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 34 cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-led Agriculture Committee, which held the bill, never moved it.

industries.industry: Energy derivatives traders (hedge funds, swap dealers, and trading houses)
industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from federal oversight by requiring position reporting, records open to regulators and prosecutors, and manipulation penalties of up to $1 million or triple their gains. Their gain under the status quo came from trading in markets that set what households pay for gasoline and heating fuel.

industries.industry: Oil, natural gas, coal, and electric utilities using over-the-counter derivatives
industries.note: Energy companies that legitimately used private contracts to hedge their own risks would have taken on reporting and recordkeeping duties, but honest participants also stood to benefit from markets that manipulators could not rig. The enforcement exposure fell mainly on firms taking outsized positions.

The bill would have required these facilities to keep records, report to the Commission, and publish volumes and prices. Their exemption from registration and disclosure requirements was part of what made this trading attractive to their customers.
